title: Understanding SQL Relationships, Foreign Keys and Inner Joins
summary: Builds a relational design in the SQLite playground: an orders table whose customer_id and product_id are foreign keys to customers and products, then uses INNER JOIN to merge related rows into one result. Includes a challenge to join orders with products.

concepts.heading: Restore the pencil row (mini challenge)
points: If the pencil was deleted in the previous lesson, insert it again with the full-values form: INSERT INTO products VALUES (2, 'Pencil', 0.8, 12). The four values follow the column order id, name, price, stock.

concepts.heading: The orders table and foreign keys
points: Columns: id (INT, NOT NULL, the primary key), order_number (INT), customer_id (INT) and product_id (INT).

A foreign key is a column holding the primary key value of a row in another table. It links the two tables: customer_id says which customer placed the order, product_id says which product was ordered. This is how a relationship is expressed in SQL, and it avoids copying customer or product details into every order.

Declare them with FOREIGN KEY (column) REFERENCES other_table (its_primary_key_column), one declaration per foreign key, after the column list and the PRIMARY KEY (id) line. For this lesson: FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id) and FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products (id).
Syntax errors show in the editor's output; the lecture's own typo was a curly brace used instead of a round bracket. Fix and re-run.
Show Schema (right-click the table) lists four fields: the primary key plus the two foreign keys.

concepts.heading: Inserting a related record
points: First order: INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 4362, 2, 1), meaning order id 1, order number 4362, customer id 2 (Angela Yu, 12 Sunset Drive in the sample customers table) and product id 1.
The numbers are just references; the details live in the customers and products tables and are pulled together by a join.

concepts.heading: INNER JOIN
points: JOIN combines rows from two tables. Types include LEFT, RIGHT, FULL and INNER; INNER JOIN is the most used and keeps only rows where the matching condition holds in both tables.

Structure: SELECT the wanted columns, written as table.column to say which table each comes from; FROM the table holding the foreign key; INNER JOIN the second table; ON the matching condition: foreign key = primary key of the other table.

Example result columns: orders.order_number plus customers.first_name, customers.last_name, customers.address, matched by orders.customer_id = customers.id. One result row then tells you who an order is for and where to send it.
The joined result is a temporary combined table produced by the query; the stored tables are not changed.

concepts.heading: Challenge: join orders with products
points: Swap the second table for products and select orders.order_number, products.name, products.price and products.stock.
The ON condition becomes orders.product_id = products.id. The result shows the order number alongside the product details.
A prebuilt copy of the full database (customers, products, orders) is linked in the lesson resources for experimenting.

task.name: Join orders with products
task.starting_point: customers, products (with stock column) and orders tables, with one order (4362, customer 2, product 1).
task.goal: Produce a result containing the order number with the product's name, price and stock.
steps: Start from the customers join query.
Replace the selected columns with orders.order_number, products.name, products.price, products.stock.
Replace the joined table with products.
Change the ON condition to orders.product_id = products.id and run.
task.expected_result: One row: order number 4362 with the name, price and stock of product 1.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 32 - SQL/32.05 Understanding SQL Relationships, Foreign Keys and Inner Joins/README.md (text only)

pitfalls: Syntax slips such as the wrong bracket type stop CREATE TABLE from running; read the error message.
Mismatched ON condition: it must pair the foreign key with the other table's primary key.
Column names without a table prefix can be ambiguous when both tables share names (such as id).
(Extra) The lecture says the order is for a pencil, but product id 1 is the Pen; the data and the spoken description disagree, so trust the ids.
(Extra) SQLite does not enforce foreign keys unless PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; PostgreSQL does.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'SQL relationships and joins': blurb on splitting data across tables. Tasks: (1) create orders with two foreign keys, (2) insert two orders, (3) INNER JOIN customers, (4) INNER JOIN products, (5) join all three tables in one query.
Starter code: customers, products and orders pre-created so the learner focuses on joins.
Demo idea: a visual three-table diagram where hovering an orders row draws arrows to the matching customers and products rows and shows the joined output row.
